Yes, a 20,000 mAh power bank is allowed on a US flight, but only in your carry-on, never in checked baggage.

**Why it qualifies:** The FAA limits spare lithium-ion batteries and power banks to 100 Wh each. To convert, divide mAh by 1000 and multiply by the voltage ([FAA: Airline Passengers and Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/airline-passengers-and-batteries)). Most power banks use 3.7 V cells, so 20 Ah × 3.7 V ≈ 74 Wh, well under the limit. Check the label on yours, since newer banks often print the Wh rating.

**Rules to follow** ([FAA PackSafe: Lithium Batteries](https://www.faa.gov/hazmat/packsafe/more_info/?hazmat=7)):
- **Carry-on only.** Spare lithium batteries and power banks are prohibited in checked bags.
- **Gate-checked bags.** If your carry-on is checked at the gate, take the power bank out and keep it with you in the cabin.
- **Protect the terminals.** Keep it in its retail packaging, a pouch, or a case, or tape over exposed terminals so nothing short-circuits.
- **Don't fly with a damaged or recalled bank.** The FAA prohibits these in both carry-on and checked bags.
- **Airline limits.** Many airlines cap how many power banks you can carry, regardless of capacity. Check your carrier's policy before you travel.
- **If it overheats.** Tell the flight crew immediately if it gets hot, swells, or smokes.

IATA gives the same guidance for international travel: keep power banks in your hand baggage and confirm your airline's policy ([IATA](https://www.iata.org/en/youandiata/travelers/batteries/)). Rules on international routes can be stricter, so check those separately.
